title: Concurrency & Deadlocks
tagline: Shared state, race conditions, and why threads freeze

sections.content:
Modern programs do many things at once. Your browser renders HTML, runs JavaScript, decodes a video, and listens for network packets — all simultaneously. Your web server handles thousands of simultaneous HTTP requests. Your database commits one transaction while three others are waiting. **Concurrency** is the art of managing multiple streams of execution, and it is one of the richest, most subtle areas in all of software engineering.

The central challenge of concurrency is **shared mutable state**: when two threads both read and write the same piece of memory, the order in which they do so is not guaranteed by the hardware — and small changes in timing can produce completely different results. This class of bug is called a **race condition**, and race conditions are notorious for being intermittent, environment-dependent, and nearly impossible to reproduce in a debugger.

The solution is **synchronization** — imposing an ordering on thread accesses using primitives such as **mutexes** and **semaphores**. But synchronization introduces its own hazard: **deadlock**. When Thread A holds Lock 1 and waits for Lock 2, while Thread B holds Lock 2 and waits for Lock 1, both threads are frozen forever — waiting for each other, going nowhere, consuming no CPU yet making no progress. Systems that deadlock silently hang, often in production, with no error message to guide you.

This chapter builds the complete mental model: what concurrency means, why race conditions happen at the hardware level, how mutexes and semaphores work mechanically, how deadlock forms and what four conditions must be present for it to occur, and the practical arsenal of strategies — prevention, detection, and avoidance — that systems designers use to tame it. These ideas underpin operating systems, databases, web servers, and any program that does more than one thing at a time.

  B --> C{"Synchronized?"}

  C -- "Yes" --> E["Critical Section\nprotected by lock"]

sections.title: The Single-Lane Bridge and the Traffic-Light
sections.content:
Picture a narrow mountain bridge wide enough for exactly one car. Cars arrive from both directions. Without any traffic control, two cars enter simultaneously from opposite ends — now neither can pass, neither will reverse first, and the road is blocked forever. That is a **deadlock**: each car holds the resource it is on (one half of the bridge) and waits for the resource the other car holds.

The bridge itself is a **critical section** — a shared resource that only one actor should use at a time. A **mutex** (mutual exclusion lock) is the traffic light at each end: before entering, a car must get a green light (acquire the lock). While that car is crossing, all lights on the other end stay red (other threads block). When the car exits, it triggers green for the other side (releases the lock). Only one car crosses at a time. No collision. No deadlock.

A **semaphore** is a more nuanced version: imagine a car park with exactly N spaces. A counter above the entrance shows how many spaces remain. Each entering car decrements the counter; each leaving car increments it. When the counter reaches zero, cars queue at the gate until someone leaves. This allows up to N cars simultaneously — a generalization of the binary one-at-a-time rule of the mutex.

The **race condition** analogy: imagine two accountants both reading the balance sheet (value: £1000) at the same time, both subtracting £200, and both writing their result back independently. The final balance reads £800 — one of the £200 withdrawals was simply overwritten, lost without a trace. The correct answer is £600. The accountants raced each other on the shared ledger and produced a wrong answer. Neither one did anything individually wrong — the problem was the lack of coordination.

sections.title: Race Conditions: How They Happen at the Hardware Level
sections.content:
A race condition is not a programming mistake in the obvious sense — it often happens in code that looks completely correct when read line by line. The problem is that what looks like one operation in source code may compile to **multiple machine instructions**, and the operating system's scheduler can interrupt a thread between any two of them.

Consider the classic counter increment: `balance = balance + 1`. In machine code, this is three instructions: (1) **LOAD** the value from memory into a CPU register, (2) **ADD** 1 to the register, (3) **STORE** the register back to memory. The scheduler can preempt a thread after step 1 or step 2 — right in the middle of what you thought was one operation.

So Thread A reads `balance = 5` into its register. The scheduler switches to Thread B. Thread B reads `balance = 5` into its own register, adds 1, writes `balance = 6`. The scheduler switches back to Thread A. Thread A adds 1 to its stale register value (still 5) and writes `balance = 6`. Both threads incremented — but the balance only went from 5 to 6 instead of to 7. **One increment was silently lost.**

This is called a **lost update** and it is the archetypal race condition. The window during which things can go wrong is called the **race window** — the gap between the LOAD and the STORE. The smaller the race window, the rarer the bug, but rarity does not mean impossibility. In high-throughput servers, a race window of a few nanoseconds can fire thousands of times per second.

The sequence of operations that must not be interrupted is called a **critical section**. Making a critical section **atomic** — indivisible from the perspective of other threads — is what synchronization primitives achieve. Modern CPUs provide special atomic instructions (like `compare-and-swap` / CAS) that execute the read-modify-write as a single hardware step that cannot be interrupted. Locks are typically built on top of these atomic CPU instructions.

sequenceDiagram
  participant T1 as "Thread 1"
  participant M as "Memory (balance=5)"
  participant T2 as "Thread 2"
  T1->>M: LOAD balance (reads 5)
  Note over T1: preempted here
  T2->>M: LOAD balance (reads 5)
  T2->>T2: ADD 1 → 6
  T2->>M: STORE 6
  Note over T1: resumes with stale value 5
  T1->>T1: ADD 1 → 6
  T1->>M: STORE 6 (overwrites T2's write!)
  Note over M: Expected 7, got 6 — lost update
sections.caption: Thread 1 is preempted between LOAD and STORE. Thread 2 completes its full increment. Thread 1 resumes with a stale value and overwrites Thread 2's result — a classic race condition producing a lost update.

sections.title: Mutexes: Binary Locks for Critical Sections
sections.content:
A **mutex** (short for mutual exclusion) is the most fundamental synchronization primitive. It has two operations: **lock** (also called `acquire`) and **unlock** (also called `release`). A mutex is in one of two states: held or free.

When a thread calls `lock()` on a free mutex, it acquires it and proceeds. The mutex is now held. If another thread calls `lock()` on the same mutex while it is held, that thread **blocks** — it is suspended by the OS and placed in a wait queue. It will not run again until the mutex is released. When the holding thread calls `unlock()`, one waiting thread is woken. (Many implementations, including Linux futex-based mutexes, wake a waiter and let it compete for the lock again rather than handing ownership over directly — faster, but not strictly FIFO-fair.)

The code between `lock()` and `unlock()` is the **critical section**. Only one thread can be inside it at any moment — the invariant guaranteed by the mutex. This is why operations inside the critical section are effectively atomic with respect to other threads competing on the same mutex.

Three properties a correct mutual-exclusion solution must provide (the classic textbook criteria):
- **Mutual exclusion**: at most one thread holds the mutex at any time (the core guarantee).
- **Progress**: if no thread holds the mutex and some threads are waiting, one will eventually acquire it.
- **Bounded waiting**: no thread waits forever (fairness — important to prevent **starvation**, where a thread is perpetually beaten to the lock by others).

**How a modern mutex is built:** the uncontended path never enters the kernel. Locking is one atomic compare-and-swap on a word in user memory (tens of nanoseconds); only if the lock is already held does the thread spin briefly and then sleep via a system call (`futex` on Linux, `WaitOnAddress` on Windows, `os_unfair_lock` on macOS). That is why uncontended locks are cheap and *contended* locks are what hurt.

A subtlety: **mutex ownership**. In most operating systems, a mutex is *owned* by the thread that locked it — only that thread can unlock it. This is unlike a binary semaphore, where any thread can signal. This ownership property makes mutexes natural for protecting critical sections that a single thread enters and exits.

**Recursive mutexes** (also called reentrant mutexes) allow the same thread to lock the same mutex multiple times without deadlocking itself — it keeps a count and only truly releases when the count drops to zero. This is useful but can mask bugs, so use with care.

sections.title: Semaphores: Counting Concurrency
sections.content:
A **semaphore** is a generalization of the mutex concept invented by Edsger Dijkstra in 1965. Instead of a binary state (held/free), a semaphore maintains an **integer count** initialized to some value N. It has two atomic operations:

- **`wait()` (also called `P`, `down`, or `acquire`)**: decrement the count. If the count is already 0, block until it becomes positive.
- **`signal()` (also called `V`, `up`, or `release`)**: increment the count. If any threads are blocked on `wait()`, wake one of them.

With N=1, a semaphore behaves like a mutex (allowing exactly one thread through at a time). With N=10, it allows up to 10 threads through simultaneously — perfect for a **connection pool** where you have 10 database connections and want at most 10 concurrent database operations.

Semaphores have two principal use cases:

**Resource counting** — the N>1 case above. You have a finite supply of some resource (connections, file descriptors, worker threads) and want to prevent oversubscription. The semaphore count represents available units.

**Signaling between threads** — initializing a semaphore to 0 and having one thread `wait()` while another `signal()`s it creates a simple one-shot event notification. The consumer blocks until the producer has finished some work. This is a building block for producer-consumer queues.

The difference in semantics from a mutex is important: a semaphore does **not have an owner**. Any thread can call `signal()`, even one that never called `wait()`. This flexibility enables signaling patterns but also means semaphores can be misused more easily than mutexes.

flowchart LR
  subgraph SEM ["Semaphore N=3"]
    C["Count = 3"]
  end
  T1["Thread 1\nwait() → count=2"] --> SEM
  T2["Thread 2\nwait() → count=1"] --> SEM
  T3["Thread 3\nwait() → count=0"] --> SEM
  T4["Thread 4\nwait() → BLOCKS"] --> SEM
  SEM --> R["3 DB Connections\n(shared resource pool)"]
sections.caption: A counting semaphore initialized to 3 allows exactly 3 threads through concurrently — ideal for limiting access to a fixed-size resource pool like database connections.

sections.title: Condition Variables and Monitors: Waiting for a State Change
sections.content:
Mutexes answer "only one at a time"; they do not answer "wait until the queue is non-empty". Spinning on `while (queue.isEmpty()) {}` burns a core, and sleeping without the lock risks a **lost wakeup** (the producer signals between your check and your sleep). A **condition variable** solves this. It is always used together with a mutex:

- `wait(cv, mutex)` **atomically** releases the mutex and puts the thread to sleep; when woken, it re-acquires the mutex before returning.
- `signal`/`notify` wakes one waiter; `broadcast`/`notify_all` wakes all of them.

The golden rule: **always re-check the condition in a `while` loop, never an `if`.** Most implementations (POSIX, Java, Python, C++) use *Mesa semantics*: a woken thread merely becomes runnable, and by the time it re-acquires the mutex another thread may already have taken the item. Implementations are also allowed **spurious wakeups** — returning from `wait` with no signal at all.

A **monitor** is a mutex plus its condition variables packaged with the data they protect. Java builds it into every object (`synchronized` + `wait()`/`notify()`), and C++ pairs `std::mutex` with `std::condition_variable`. A semaphore can express similar signalling, but a condition variable can wait on *any* predicate over the shared state, not just a counter.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
import collections
import threading


class BoundedQueue:
    """A monitor: one lock plus two condition variables guarding a deque."""

    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.items = collections.deque()
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
        self.not_full = threading.Condition(self.lock)
        self.not_empty = threading.Condition(self.lock)

    def put(self, item):
        with self.lock:
            while len(self.items) >= self.capacity:  # `while`, never `if`
                self.not_full.wait()                 # atomically unlock + sleep, relock on wake
            self.items.append(item)
            self.not_empty.notify()                  # wake one waiting consumer

    def get(self):
        with self.lock:
            while not self.items:
                self.not_empty.wait()
            item = self.items.popleft()
            self.not_full.notify()                   # a slot opened: wake one producer
            return item


q = BoundedQueue(capacity=2)
results = []


def producer():
    for i in range(5):
        q.put(i)       # blocks whenever 2 items are already waiting
    q.put(None)        # sentinel: no more items


def consumer():
    while (item := q.get()) is not None:
        results.append(item)


threads = [threading.Thread(target=producer), threading.Thread(target=consumer)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print(results)  # [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
sections.explanation: Python's `threading.Condition` is a condition variable bound to a lock. `wait()` releases the lock while sleeping and re-acquires it before returning, which is why the producer can make progress while the consumer waits. The `while` loops re-check the predicate after every wake-up, covering both spurious wakeups and the case where another thread consumed the item first. With capacity 2 the producer blocks repeatedly — that is the bounded buffer applying backpressure.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The race is deterministic here: both withdrawals read 1000 before either writes, so the last writer wins and one withdrawal vanishes. The async mutex chains each task onto the previous one, so the second withdrawal only reads `balance` after the first has written it. The `run.catch(() => {})` line matters: without it, one rejected task would leave the chain rejected and every later task would be skipped. The semaphore keeps a FIFO queue of waiting resolvers — `signal()` hands a free slot directly to the next waiter — and the `finally` block guarantees release even when the operation throws.

sections.title: Deadlock: The Four Coffman Conditions
sections.content:
**Deadlock** is a state in which a set of threads are all blocked, each waiting for a resource held by another thread in the set. No thread can make progress. The system is frozen. Deadlock is not a crash — the threads are still alive, consuming memory, holding locks — they simply never do anything useful again.

In 1971, Edward Coffman and colleagues identified four conditions that must **all** hold simultaneously for deadlock to occur — they are *necessary* conditions. (When every resource has a single instance, as with ordinary locks, a circular wait under the other three conditions *is* a deadlock; with multi-instance resources a cycle can exist without one.) Understanding each condition is the key to preventing deadlock:

**Condition 1 — Mutual Exclusion**: At least one resource must be held in a non-shareable mode. Only one thread can use the resource at a time; if another thread requests it, it must wait. This is a fundamental property of locks — you cannot simply remove it without giving up the protection that locks provide.

**Condition 2 — Hold and Wait**: A thread must be holding at least one resource and simultaneously waiting to acquire additional resources that are currently held by other threads. This is the natural behavior of any program that needs two locks at once — it acquires the first, then tries for the second while keeping the first.

**Condition 3 — No Preemption**: Resources cannot be forcibly taken away from a thread that holds them. A thread releases a resource only voluntarily, after it has completed its task. Locks cannot normally be snatched by the OS from a live thread — this would corrupt any computation the thread was protecting.

**Condition 4 — Circular Wait**: There must exist a cycle in the **resource-wait graph**: Thread A waits for a resource held by Thread B, which waits for a resource held by Thread C, which waits for a resource held by Thread A (or more directly, A waits for B and B waits for A). Without a cycle, at least one thread in any chain can proceed, and eventually all threads can proceed.

The profound insight: breaking **any one** of these four conditions makes deadlock impossible. Each condition corresponds to a different prevention strategy — and each strategy has different costs and tradeoffs.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  ME["1. Mutual Exclusion\nResource held exclusively"] --> DL["DEADLOCK"]
  HW["2. Hold and Wait\nHolding lock while waiting"] --> DL
  NP["3. No Preemption\nLocks not forcibly taken"] --> DL
  CW["4. Circular Wait\nA waits B waits A"] --> DL
  DL --> P1["Break CW: Lock Ordering"]
  DL --> P2["Break HW: Acquire All at Once"]
  DL --> P3["Break NP: Timeout + Release"]
  DL --> P4["Avoid: Banker's Algorithm"]
sections.caption: All four Coffman conditions must hold simultaneously for deadlock. Each prevention strategy targets one condition.

sections.title: The Resource-Wait Graph: Visualizing Deadlock
sections.content:
A **resource-allocation graph** is the formal tool for reasoning about deadlock. It is a directed graph with two types of nodes: **threads** (circles) and **resources** (squares). Two types of directed edges exist:

- **Assignment edge**: resource R → thread T (R is currently held by T)
- **Request edge**: thread T → resource R (T is waiting for R)

Collapsing the resource nodes gives the simpler **wait-for graph**: an edge T1 → T2 whenever T1 waits for a lock T2 holds. When each resource has a single instance (true for ordinary locks), **a deadlock exists if and only if there is a cycle in this graph**; with multi-instance resources a cycle is necessary but not sufficient. This makes deadlock detection algorithmic: periodically scan the wait-for graph and look for cycles. If you find one, you have a deadlock, and you know exactly which threads and resources are involved.

For the simple two-thread deadlock: Thread A → Lock B (A waiting for B), Lock B → Thread B (B holds Lock B), Thread B → Lock A (B waiting for A), Lock A → Thread A (A holds Lock A). The cycle A→B→A is immediately visible.

In a database system, this is exactly what the lock manager does. PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB and SQL Server all keep wait-for information and look for cycles, then abort a **victim** transaction. InnoDB checks as soon as a transaction starts waiting and rolls back the one that has modified the fewest rows; PostgreSQL waits `deadlock_timeout` (1 s by default) before running its detector and aborts the transaction that ran it; SQL Server's background monitor picks the cheapest victim unless `DEADLOCK_PRIORITY` says otherwise. This is why you see errors such as PostgreSQL's `deadlock detected` or SQL Server's "…chosen as the deadlock victim. Rerun the transaction."

In application code, wait-for graphs are rarely maintained explicitly. Instead, developers rely on **prevention strategies** (discussed next) to ensure cycles never form, rather than detecting and recovering from them after the fact.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  T1["Thread A"] -- "holds" --> LA["Lock 1"]
  T1 -- "waits for" --> LB["Lock 2"]
  T2["Thread B"] -- "holds" --> LB
  T2 -- "waits for" --> LA
  LA -- "held by" --> T1
  LB -- "held by" --> T2
sections.caption: Resource-wait graph showing a classic two-thread deadlock. The cycle Thread A → Lock 2 → Thread B → Lock 1 → Thread A confirms deadlock.

sections.title: Prevention Strategy 1: Lock Ordering (Breaking Circular Wait)
sections.content:
**Lock ordering** is the most widely deployed deadlock prevention technique because it has zero runtime overhead and is simple to reason about. The rule: **assign a total ordering to all locks in the system, and require every thread to acquire locks in ascending order of that ranking**.

Why does this work? If every thread always acquires Lock 1 before Lock 2 before Lock 3 (by their global rank), then a circular wait cannot form. To have a cycle, Thread A would need to hold a higher-ranked lock and wait for a lower-ranked one — but the ordering rule forbids acquiring a lower-ranked lock after a higher-ranked one. The cycle is structurally impossible.

In practice, locks are often ranked by the ID of the resource they protect. A bank transfer function between accounts always acquires the lock on the lower account ID first. The same trick prevents most database deadlocks: transactions that update several rows should touch them in a consistent primary-key order (for example `SELECT … ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE`).

The challenge: lock ordering requires **global knowledge**. Every developer writing code that acquires multiple locks must know the ordering. This is a documentation and discipline problem. Some systems enforce it automatically by wrapping lock objects in a class that tracks the current thread's last acquired rank and panics if you try to acquire a lower-ranked one; the Linux kernel's `lockdep` validator checks lock ordering at runtime and reports a violation the first time it happens, even if no deadlock occurred.

Lock ordering is practical, zero-cost at runtime, and the right default choice for most systems.

sections.title: Prevention Strategy 2: Acquire All Locks Atomically (Breaking Hold and Wait)
sections.content:
The **Hold and Wait** condition can be broken by requiring that a thread acquires **all the locks it will ever need before it begins executing**, and either gets all of them or none of them. This is called **all-or-nothing lock acquisition**.

If a thread cannot get all its required locks at once, it releases any it did manage to acquire and tries again later. This eliminates the scenario of holding Lock 1 while waiting for Lock 2, because you either hold both or you hold neither.

The downside is **reduced concurrency**: the thread holds all locks for its entire computation, preventing others from using resources that the thread only needs briefly at the end. It also requires threads to know in advance which resources they will need — not always possible if resource requirements depend on intermediate computations.

In databases the corresponding idea is **conservative (static) two-phase locking**: a transaction acquires every lock it needs before it starts, so it can never deadlock. Ordinary (strict) **2PL** — acquire locks as you go, release them only at commit — guarantees serializability but does **not** prevent deadlock, which is exactly why databases also run the deadlock detector described above.

sections.title: Prevention Strategy 3: Timeout and Retry (Breaking No Preemption)
sections.content:
**No Preemption** can be broken by giving threads a way to voluntarily surrender their locks when they cannot make progress. The most practical implementation is **lock timeout with retry**: instead of blocking indefinitely on `lock()`, use `tryLock(timeout)`. If the lock cannot be acquired within the timeout, release all currently held locks and retry the entire operation after a random backoff.

The random backoff is important: if two threads both time out simultaneously and both retry immediately, they may deadlock again. Adding randomness (jitter) breaks this symmetry — one will succeed before the other.

This strategy breaks the No Preemption condition because the thread *itself* voluntarily releases resources when progress is impossible — it is effectively self-preempting. The weakness is **livelock**: threads may keep timing out and retrying indefinitely without making progress, consuming CPU without doing useful work. Exponential backoff (doubling the wait time after each failure) mitigates livelock.

Classic shared-medium Ethernet (CSMA/CD) is the famous real-world example: after the n-th collision a sender waits a random number of slot times between 0 and 2ⁿ − 1 (binary exponential backoff). Modern switched, full-duplex Ethernet has no collisions, but the same pattern lives on in Wi-Fi and in retry logic for distributed systems.

sections.title: Avoidance: The Banker's Algorithm
sections.content:
Deadlock **avoidance** differs from prevention: rather than breaking Coffman conditions structurally, avoidance dynamically decides whether to grant a resource request based on whether granting it could lead to deadlock.

The classic avoidance algorithm is Dijkstra's **Banker's Algorithm** (1965), named by analogy to a bank that grants loans only when it knows it can satisfy all potential future demands. Before granting a resource request, the algorithm asks: "If I grant this request, is the resulting state **safe**?" A state is safe if there exists an ordering in which all threads can eventually run to completion (called a **safe sequence**).

To check safety, the algorithm simulates finishing threads one by one: find a thread whose remaining resource needs can be satisfied by currently available resources, simulate it finishing and releasing all its resources, then repeat with the remaining threads. If all threads can be finished this way, the state is safe. If the grant would produce an unsafe state, the request is deferred (the thread blocks) even if the resource is currently available.

The Banker's Algorithm is theoretically elegant but has significant practical limitations:
- It requires threads to **declare their maximum resource needs** in advance — often impractical.
- It assumes a **fixed number of threads** — real systems spawn and destroy threads dynamically.
- Each safety check costs **O(m × n²)** for n threads and m resource types, and it runs on every request — fine for small systems, prohibitive for thousands of threads.

For these reasons, the Banker's Algorithm is rarely used in practice (except in some real-time and embedded operating systems where resources and tasks are known statically). In most real systems, deadlock prevention (lock ordering) is preferred over avoidance.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: `transferSafe` eliminates deadlock by lock ordering: every caller locks the lower-ID account first, so a cycle in the wait-for graph is impossible — and nested `try/finally` blocks release both locks even if the update throws. `transferWithTimeout` never waits indefinitely while holding a lock: if it cannot get the second lock in time, the `finally` releases the first, then it backs off exponentially with random jitter so two competing threads do not retry in lockstep (livelock).

sections.title: Starvation and Livelock: The Other Concurrency Hazards
sections.content:
Deadlock is not the only way concurrency can go wrong at the lock level. Two closely related problems are often conflated with deadlock but are distinct:

**Starvation** occurs when a thread is perpetually denied access to a resource it needs, even though no deadlock exists. Threads do make progress — just not *this* thread. The classic cause is priority scheduling: if high-priority threads continuously acquire a lock before a low-priority thread gets the chance, the low-priority thread may wait indefinitely. Fairness mechanisms — like FIFO lock queues (the next thread to wait is the next to get the lock) or **priority inheritance** (temporarily boosting a low-priority thread's priority when it holds a lock that a high-priority thread needs) — prevent starvation.

**Livelock** is the ironic cousin of deadlock. Threads are not blocked — they are actively running — but they are caught in a loop of actions and reactions that prevent any of them from making progress. Think of two people in a narrow corridor: each steps to the right to let the other pass, they face each other again, each steps left, and so on indefinitely. Both are moving, neither is getting past. The timeout-and-retry approach is vulnerable to livelock if all conflicting threads consistently time out and retry at the same time. Exponential backoff with random jitter is the standard cure.

**Priority inversion** is a particularly dangerous hazard in real-time systems. A high-priority thread H waits for a lock held by low-priority thread L. Meanwhile, a medium-priority thread M (which does not need the lock) runs instead of L, because M has higher priority than L. H is blocked waiting for L, but L cannot run because M preempts it. H is effectively running at L's priority — it is inverted. The Mars Pathfinder mission in 1997 famously experienced this bug, causing the spacecraft's computer to reset repeatedly. The fix — priority inheritance — was applied remotely from Earth.

sections.title: Atomic Operations and Lock-Free Data Structures
sections.content:
For performance-critical code, taking and releasing locks — even uncontested ones — has overhead: cache line invalidation, memory barriers, potential OS context switches. **Lock-free** (and **wait-free**) programming uses **hardware atomic operations** to build concurrent data structures without locks.

The fundamental atomic primitive on modern CPUs is **Compare-And-Swap (CAS)**: atomically compare a memory location to an expected value, and if equal, replace it with a new value; return whether the swap succeeded. On x86 this is a single instruction (`LOCK CMPXCHG`); on ARM it is either a load-exclusive/store-exclusive pair (`LDXR`/`STXR`) or, since ARMv8.1, a single `CAS` instruction.

CAS enables a **retry loop** (sometimes called optimistic concurrency): read the current value, compute the desired new value, CAS from old to new. If the CAS fails (because another thread changed the value between your read and your CAS), retry. This is correct because a failed CAS means someone else already made progress — the overall system is not stuck.

Lock-free stacks, queues, and hash maps are built this way. JavaScript's `Atomics` API (for SharedArrayBuffer) exposes these primitives. Java's `java.util.concurrent.atomic` package (AtomicInteger, AtomicReference) provides CAS-based counters and references. Most modern runtime systems use CAS extensively in their garbage collectors and memory allocators.

The tradeoff: lock-free code is **much harder to write correctly** than mutex-protected code. The ABA problem (a value changes A→B→A between your read and your CAS, so the CAS succeeds even though the structure changed underneath — for example a node was freed and its address reused; see the Lock-Free Programming topic) is a classic pitfall. For application-level code, using well-tested concurrent data structures from a standard library is almost always the right choice over hand-written lock-free code.

**Historical context:** The deadlock problem was formally identified in the early 1960s as time-sharing operating systems began allowing multiple programs to run concurrently. Edsger Dijkstra formalized the semaphore concept in 1965 and posed the Dining Philosophers problem (later named by Tony Hoare) — five philosophers alternately thinking and eating, sharing five forks between them — as a precise demonstration of how deadlock arises and how to prevent it. The Coffman conditions were published in 1971. Dijkstra described the Banker's Algorithm in the same period (EWD 108). These foundational ideas are now 60 years old and still directly applicable to every concurrent system built today.

**Common mistakes and interview insights:**
- **Forgetting to release locks on the error path**: always use try/finally (or RAII in C++) to guarantee unlock even when an exception is thrown.
- **Holding locks too long**: minimize the critical section. If you hold a lock while doing I/O or an HTTP call, you are blocking every other thread for the entire network round-trip.
- **Using the wrong primitive**: use a mutex when ownership matters (one thread acquires and releases); use a semaphore for counting or signaling between different threads.
- **Lock ordering is the interview answer**: when asked 'how do you prevent deadlock?', the expected answer is consistent global lock ordering to eliminate circular wait — it is simple, zero-overhead, and universally applicable.
- **Databases detect deadlocks and kill victims**: if your transaction is aborted with a deadlock error, always retry it — the database chose your transaction as the cheapest to restart.
- **JavaScript is single-threaded but async code has races**: shared state mutated across `await` boundaries can race — the event loop switches tasks at every `await`. An async mutex (promise chain) is the JS equivalent of a mutex lock.

items: A **race condition** occurs when multiple threads access shared mutable state without synchronization; the OS can preempt a thread between any two machine instructions, corrupting multi-step operations like read-modify-write.

A **mutex** provides mutual exclusion — only one thread can hold it at a time, protecting a critical section; a **semaphore** is a generalized counter allowing up to N concurrent accesses, used for resource pools and thread signaling.

A **condition variable** lets a thread sleep until shared state changes: `wait()` atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, and the condition must be re-checked in a `while` loop (Mesa semantics, spurious wakeups). Mutex + condition variables = a **monitor**.

**Deadlock** requires all four Coffman conditions simultaneously (they are necessary conditions): Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait — breaking any one prevents deadlock.
**Lock ordering** (always acquiring locks in a consistent global order) eliminates Circular Wait at zero runtime cost and is the most practical deadlock prevention technique in real systems.
**Timeout and retry** (with exponential backoff and jitter) breaks No Preemption by having threads voluntarily release locks when they cannot make progress — but risks livelock without the jitter.

The **Banker's Algorithm** avoids deadlock by only granting resource requests that keep the system in a safe state, but requires advance knowledge of maximum needs and is rarely practical outside embedded systems.

**Starvation**, **livelock**, and **priority inversion** are related concurrency hazards: starvation means one thread never gets the lock; livelock means threads loop without progress; priority inversion can be as dangerous as deadlock in real-time systems (see: Mars Pathfinder 1997).

quiz.question: A race condition on a counter occurs because `balance = balance + 1` compiles to three machine instructions. Which instruction ordering allows a lost update?
options: Thread A executes LOAD, is preempted, Thread B executes all three, Thread A resumes and writes a stale value
Thread A completes all three instructions before Thread B starts any
Both threads execute STORE simultaneously, and the CPU averages the two values
The OS detects the conflict and rolls back one thread automatically
quiz.explanation: After Thread A's LOAD, the scheduler can switch to Thread B, which completes the full read-modify-write and writes the incremented value. Thread A resumes with its register still holding the old value, computes old+1, and overwrites Thread B's result — a lost update.

quiz.question: Which property distinguishes a mutex from a binary semaphore?
options: A mutex allows up to 2 threads in the critical section; a semaphore allows only 1
A mutex is owned by the thread that locked it — only that thread can unlock it; a semaphore has no owner
A semaphore uses hardware atomic instructions; a mutex uses software spin-waiting
They are functionally identical — the names are historical synonyms
quiz.explanation: Mutex ownership is the critical distinction: only the acquiring thread may release a mutex, making it appropriate for protecting critical sections. A binary semaphore has no owner — any thread can signal it — which enables producer-consumer signaling patterns but makes it easier to misuse.

quiz.question: A semaphore is initialized to 3. Threads T1, T2, T3, and T4 each call wait(). What happens to T4?
options: T4 proceeds immediately because the semaphore counter wraps to 0
T4 steals the semaphore from the lowest-priority thread
T4 raises an exception because the count cannot go negative
T4 blocks until one of T1, T2, or T3 calls signal()
quiz.explanation: T1, T2, T3 each decrement the counter (3→2→1→0). When T4 calls wait(), the count is 0 and T4 blocks. It will unblock only when one of the other threads calls signal(), incrementing the count back to 1.

quiz.question: Which statement about the four Coffman conditions is correct?
options: Mutual exclusion alone is enough to cause deadlock
Circular wait alone causes deadlock even if resources can be preempted
All four are necessary — if any one of them is prevented, deadlock cannot occur
Any two of the four conditions together guarantee deadlock
quiz.explanation: The Coffman conditions are necessary conditions: deadlock can only occur when mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait all hold at the same time. That is why each prevention strategy needs to break just one of them. With single-instance resources such as ordinary locks, a cycle under the other three conditions is a deadlock.

quiz.question: Thread A holds Lock 1 and waits for Lock 2. Thread B holds Lock 2 and waits for Lock 1. Which Coffman condition does this scenario most directly illustrate?
options: No Preemption — neither thread can be forced to release its lock
Hold and Wait — both threads hold a resource while waiting for another
Circular Wait — Thread A waits for B's resource, B waits for A's resource
Mutual Exclusion — each lock can only be held by one thread
quiz.explanation: The defining characteristic of this scenario is the cycle in the wait-for graph: A→Lock2→B→Lock1→A. That cycle is precisely the Circular Wait condition. Hold and Wait and No Preemption are also present, but Circular Wait is the most direct description of this pattern.

quiz.question: Why does always acquiring locks in ascending ID order prevent deadlock?
options: It makes Circular Wait structurally impossible, because no thread ever waits for a lower-ranked lock it does not hold
It eliminates Mutual Exclusion, so no thread has exclusive access
It eliminates Hold and Wait, because threads acquire only one lock at a time
It enables the OS to preempt locks from threads when needed
quiz.explanation: Lock ordering breaks the Circular Wait condition. For a cycle to exist, some thread would need to hold a higher-ranked lock while waiting for a lower-ranked one. The ordering rule forbids this — every thread always waits for higher-ranked locks — so no cycle can form.

quiz.question: In the async JavaScript race condition example, why does the mutex (promise chaining) fix the lost-update bug?
options: It makes the arithmetic operation atomic at the CPU level
It forces each withdrawal to complete (including its await) before the next one reads balance
It prevents the event loop from switching tasks during synchronous code
It copies the balance into a local variable before the await
quiz.explanation: The promise chain serializes execution: the second withdrawal's function is only invoked after the first withdrawal's promise fully resolves (after its await). So the second withdrawal always reads the balance that reflects the first withdrawal's STORE — the read-modify-write is effectively atomic at the async level.

quiz.question: The Banker's Algorithm is classified as deadlock ___. What does it do?
options: Prevention — it removes Mutual Exclusion from the system
Detection — it scans the wait-for graph for cycles periodically
Recovery — it aborts the cheapest deadlocked thread to break the cycle
Avoidance — it only grants resource requests that leave the system in a safe state
quiz.explanation: The Banker's Algorithm is deadlock avoidance: before granting any resource request, it simulates the resulting state and checks whether a safe execution ordering still exists. If granting the request would lead to an unsafe state, it defers the request — even if the resource is available.

quiz.question: What is livelock, and how does it differ from deadlock?
options: Livelock is when threads are blocked waiting for each other; deadlock is when they are busy-waiting
Livelock is when threads are actively running but making no progress due to reactive behavior; deadlock is when threads are completely blocked
Livelock means exactly two threads are stuck; deadlock can involve any number
They are the same phenomenon — livelock is the modern term for deadlock
quiz.explanation: In livelock, threads are not blocked — they are running and responding to each other — but their responses keep undoing each other's progress. The classic example is the timeout-and-retry loop where both threads time out simultaneously and retry simultaneously indefinitely. Deadlock means threads are blocked and cannot run at all.

quiz.question: A database aborts your transaction with the message 'Deadlock detected — your transaction was chosen as the victim.' What should you do?
options: Retry the transaction from the beginning — the database has already released your locks
Terminate the connection — the database is in an inconsistent state
Wait for the other transaction to finish before retrying — the lock will be available
Switch to a different database node — this node has a corrupted lock table
quiz.explanation: When the database detects a deadlock cycle, it aborts one transaction (the 'victim') and rolls it back completely, releasing all its locks. The victim transaction can safely be retried from scratch. The other transaction in the cycle is allowed to complete. Retrying is the standard and correct response to a deadlock victim error.
